posts.title: Pressing the last cosmos of the year
posts.excerpt: Frost is two weeks away, so every cosmos left on the flower table goes into the press. Here is how Jun does it, and how you can at home.
posts.content:
The first frost usually reaches Ashcombe in the last week of October. Until then the cosmos keep coming, and by the end of each week a few stems are left on the table, a little too open to send out. They do not go in the bin. They go into the press.

Blotting paper, a heavy book, patience

Jun Okada runs the pressing room at the back of the shop. Each flower is laid face down on blotting paper, petals spread with a dry brush, then covered with a second sheet and a stack of old atlases. The paper is changed after three days, and again after a week.

The coral fades to the colour of a seashell. That is the moment I wait for.

Jun Okada, dried flowers and wreaths

After a month they come out flat and papery, ready for frames, cards and the gift tags on our bouquets. At home, a thick book and kitchen paper do the job: choose flowers with flat faces, press them the day you pick them, and leave them alone for three weeks.

posts.title: How to keep a bouquet for ten days
posts.excerpt: Our five-day promise is the minimum. With three small habits most of our bouquets last ten days or more.
posts.content:
Every bouquet that leaves Petal Row comes with a little care card. Here is the longer version, for anyone who wants to stretch a bunch of ranunculus into a second week.

Three habits

  • Cut each stem at a slant, two centimetres up, before the first drink, and again every second day.
  • Fresh, cool water every second day, in a vase you have washed with a drop of soap.
  • Keep the vase away from the fruit bowl, radiators and sunny windowsills: ripening fruit and warmth age flowers fast.

Flowers drink like we do: little and often, and never from a dirty glass.

Mina Hart, florist

Ranunculus and roses open slowly over the first days; that is the best part. When the outer petals tire, take them off and the flower looks new again.

posts.title: Wreath workshops at the long table
posts.excerpt: Six winter evenings, bay and fern from the Fernbrook allotments, and a wreath of your own to take home.
posts.content:
When the growers slow down for winter, the long oak table in the back of the shop becomes a workshop. This year there are six evenings, from the second week of November.

What happens on the night

Jun shows you how to bind a frame of willow, then you build your wreath from bay, fern, rosemary and dried strawflowers. It takes about two hours, with mulled apple juice and cake halfway.

Places are limited to ten a night. Readers of the Monday letter hear about them first.

posts.title: Why we wrap in paper, not plastic
posts.excerpt: Kraft paper, cotton ribbon and a compostable water pouch: what a bouquet from us is wrapped in, and why.
posts.content:
Since 2019 nothing in our shop has been wrapped in plastic. It took a year of trying papers, ribbons and water pouches to find a wrap that keeps flowers fresh on a bicycle ride across town.

What is in the wrap

  • Unbleached kraft paper, or blush tissue for gifts.
  • A cotton ribbon: bring it back and we use it again.
  • A small pouch of water at the stems, made from plant starch, that goes in the compost.

It looks better, too. Paper lets a bouquet breathe and move.

Ravi Linde, counter and orders

posts.title: A basket for every doorstep
posts.excerpt: Why we arrange in willow baskets you keep, and how to keep a basket arrangement fresh.
posts.content:
Our shop is named after a flower basket, so baskets had to come back. The willow baskets are woven by a family workshop two valleys away, and each one has a lined pot inside so it can hold water.

Keeping a basket fresh

Top up the water every day: a basket arrangement drinks more than a vase. When the flowers are over, rinse the liner and keep the basket for bread, wool or next spring's tulips.

posts.title: Dried flowers that last all winter
posts.excerpt: Pampas, statice and strawflowers dried in the loft above the shop: how we choose them and how to keep them looking good.
posts.content:
Not every flower wants to be dried. The ones that do keep their colour for a year or more: strawflowers, statice, pampas, lavender and some hydrangeas.

Our drying loft

Above the shop is a warm, dark loft where bunches hang upside down for two to three weeks. Darkness keeps the colour; warmth and moving air keep away the mould.

At home, keep dried flowers out of direct sun and steam, and dust them now and then with a hairdryer on cool.

products.description:
Our most-loved bouquet: coral and peach ranunculus, blush garden roses and silver-dollar eucalyptus, gathered loosely so it looks freshly picked.

The ranunculus open slowly over the first days. Trim the stems and change the water every second day and it lasts well over a week.
